triarchy-of-negroponte.t: Crusader lordship on Euboea, split among three Lombard lords under the growing shadow of Venice, which eventually took over the whole island.
triarchy-of-negroponte.o: After the Fourth Crusade, Boniface of Montferrat granted Euboea in 1205 to Jacques d'Avesnes and then to Lombard nobles from Verona, notably Ravano dalle Carceri. In 1209 Ravano recognised Venetian overlordship. After his death in 1216 the island was divided into three parts, the terzieri, each held by a lord called a triarch.
triarchy-of-negroponte.r: The triarchs, of families such as the dalle Carceri and Ghisi, were vassals of the Principality of Achaea but relied on Venice, which held quarters and a bailo in the town of Negroponte (Chalcis) and controlled its trade. Greek peasants worked the land under Latin lords. The renegade knight Licario, serving Byzantium, recaptured much of the island in the 1270s.
triarchy-of-negroponte.e: Threatened by the Catalans of the Duchy of Athens and the Turks, the triarchs ceded more and more to Venice. By 1390 Venice ruled the whole island directly as Venetian Negroponte.

third-taifa-of-niebla.t: The last independent Muslim state of western al-Andalus, ruled by Ibn Mahfuz from Niebla until Alfonso X took it in 1262.
third-taifa-of-niebla.o: Around 1234, as Ibn Hud's power faded, Shuayb ibn Muhammad ibn Mahfuz established himself in Niebla and the surrounding district as an independent ruler. After Ferdinand III took Seville in 1248, he accepted Castilian overlordship and paid tribute.
third-taifa-of-niebla.r: The small realm covered Niebla, Huelva and the lower Guadiana region, protected by Niebla's massive walls. As a vassal of the Crown of Castile, Ibn Mahfuz kept internal autonomy, but his isolation between Castilian Seville and the Kingdom of Portugal left him little room to manoeuvre.
third-taifa-of-niebla.e: In 1262 Alfonso X besieged Niebla for several months, and Ibn Mahfuz surrendered in exchange for lands and income in Seville. The territory became part of Castile.

thurii.t: Panhellenic colony founded under Athenian sponsorship near ruined Sybaris in 444 BCE, linked with Herodotus and Protagoras.
thurii.o: After several attempts by Sybarite survivors to refound their city, Athens under Pericles organised a new colony open to settlers from all Greece. Thurii was founded in 444 or 443 BCE near the old site, with a street plan attributed to Hippodamus and laws attributed to Protagoras. The historian Herodotus is said to have joined it.
thurii.r: The settlers soon quarrelled; the descendants of Sybarites claimed privileges and were expelled, and the citizen body was organised in ten tribes by origin. Thurii prospered from the Sybarite plain and fought Taras over Siris, a dispute settled by the joint foundation of Heraclea in 433 BCE. Lucanian pressure grew, and in 389 BCE they crushed a Thurian army near Laus.
thurii.e: Threatened again by the Lucanians, Thurii appealed to Rome, which placed a garrison there in 282 BCE; the move provoked Taras and led to the war with Pyrrhus. Thurii later suffered in the Hannibalic War, and in 193 BCE Rome founded the Latin colony of Copia on the site.

turduli.t: A people of the south-west, close kin of the Turdetani, with a northern branch, the Turduli Veteres, living near the Douro in Portugal.
turduli.o: The Turduli lived in the middle Guadiana and Guadalquivir regions next to the Turdetani, from whom Strabo said they could hardly be distinguished. A separate group, the Turduli Veteres or Old Turduli, settled south of the lower Douro in northern Portugal, probably after migrating from the south.
turduli.r: Little is recorded of their government. Their economy relied on farming, herding and the mineral wealth of the Sierra Morena. Pliny lists their towns in both Baetica and Lusitania, which shows how widespread the group was.
turduli.e: They were absorbed into Roman Hispania Ulterior during the 2nd century BCE, following the conquest of the south after 206 BCE and the Lusitanian wars. Under Augustus their lands were divided between Baetica and Lusitania.

taifa-of-almeria.t: A wealthy port taifa famous for its silk, whose poet-king al-Mutasim ibn Sumadih made Almería a centre of Andalusi culture.
taifa-of-almeria.o: Almería had become the main naval base of the Caliphate of Córdoba. After its fall, the Amirid freedman Khayran seized the city around 1013, followed by another freedman, Zuhayr, who was killed in 1038. After a period under Valencia, the Arab Tujibid family of the Banu Sumadih took power in 1041 under Man ibn Sumadih.
taifa-of-almeria.r: Almería prospered as the busiest port of al-Andalus, trading with Egypt and the Maghreb and producing fine silks and brocades on thousands of looms. Al-Mutasim (1052-1091) enlarged the great Alcazaba and gathered poets and scholars at his court, while paying tribute to Castile and quarrelling with the Taifa of Granada.
taifa-of-almeria.e: Al-Mutasim died in 1091 as the Almoravids besieged the city, and his son fled to North Africa. Almería became an Almoravid province, briefly broke away as the Second Taifa of Almería in 1145, and then fell to Castile in 1147.

taifa-of-silves.t: A taifa in the western Algarve ruled by the Banu Muzayn from Silves, then a rich river port and later a city of poets under Seville.
taifa-of-silves.o: Around 1027 Muhammad ibn Muzayn, from a local Arab family, took control of Silves on the Arade river. The town had grown into the chief city of the Algarve, and the family ruled it as an independent principality amid the confusion following the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba.
taifa-of-silves.r: Silves, with its red sandstone castle and navigable river, traded in figs, dried fruit and timber and was known for its pure Arabic speech and poetry. The Banu Muzayn ruled a small territory and had to fend off the expanding Taifa of Seville and the neighbouring Taifa of Santa María del Algarve.
taifa-of-silves.e: In 1063 al-Mutadid of Seville annexed Silves and made his son al-Mutamid governor, with the poet Ibn Ammar at his side. The city later became the Second Taifa of Silves in 1144.

transpadane-republic.t: A French-sponsored republic in Lombardy, created after Napoleon's conquest of Milan in 1796 and the first of the Italian sister republics.
transpadane-republic.o: After defeating the Austrians at Lodi in May 1796, Napoleon Bonaparte entered Milan and ended Austrian rule in the Duchy of Milan. The French set up an administration of Lombard Jacobins and moderates, and in November 1796 Lombardy north of the Po was organised as the Transpadane Republic.
transpadane-republic.r: The republic was governed under French military control, with local administrations in Milan and the Lombard cities. It paid heavy war contributions and saw church and noble property seized and artworks shipped to Paris, but also had a lively political press and debate about Italian unity. Milan's patriots organised a competition in 1796 on the best form of free government for Italy.
transpadane-republic.e: In June and July 1797 Napoleon merged the Transpadane Republic with the Cispadane Republic and other territories to form the Cisalpine Republic, with Milan as capital.

taifa-of-moron.t: A Berber principality around Morón de la Frontera, one of the small hill-town states between Seville and Ronda that the Abbadids absorbed.
taifa-of-moron.o: Around 1013 the Banu Dammar, a Berber clan whose soldiers had served the Córdoban caliphs, took control of Morón and its district in the countryside south-east of Seville under Nuh ibn Abi Tuziri al-Dammari.
taifa-of-moron.r: Morón was a modest state built around a castle, olive groves and grain land. Its rulers allied with the Hammudids and the other Berber taifas, such as the Taifa of Carmona and the Taifa of Ronda, against the expanding Arab dynasty of Seville. Little is known of its administration.
taifa-of-moron.e: In 1066 al-Mutadid of the Taifa of Seville annexed Morón, reportedly after luring Berber rulers into a trap. The town remained Muslim until the Castilian conquest in the 13th century.

teos.t: Ionian port city, home of the poet Anacreon, whose citizens fled Persian conquest to found Abdera and which later hosted the guild of Dionysiac artists.
teos.o: Teos lay on an isthmus south-west of Smyrna and was settled by Ionians, with Boeotian and Athenian elements according to tradition, c. 1000 BCE. It joined the Ionian League, and Thales is said to have proposed Teos as the capital of a united Ionia because of its central position.
teos.r: Teos lived from trade and two harbours. When the Persian general Harpagus attacked c. 545 BCE, many citizens sailed away and founded Abdera in Thrace. Anacreon, the lyric poet, was born there. The 'Teian curses', public inscriptions of c. 470 BCE, threatened anyone who harmed the grain supply or plotted tyranny. Teos sent 17 ships to Lade in 494 BCE.
teos.e: Under the Hellenistic kings Teos built Hermogenes's great temple of Dionysus and became the seat of the Ionian-Hellespontine guild of Dionysiac artists. It passed into Roman Asia after 133 BCE.
